_meta.directives: Fiche pilote recentrée sur le nom (2026-10-03). Chaque piste d'origine est attribuée à qui la porte et citée à la page dans les notes de sa source ; aucune n'est retenue comme la bonne. Ne pas étendre sans source dédiée.

oralTraditions.claim: The name is said to come from an ancestor. The account traces the lineage to Kela Mansa Subri, a warrior from Djida, whose son Mansa Djida is said to have come to Africa; the descendants of Kamanjan Boro, son of Neni Mansa Kara, were the first to be called Kamara, and Kamanjan Boro then settled at Tabon.
oralTraditions.carrier: Babou Condé, griot du village de Fadama, dans la préfecture de Kouroussa en Guinée
oralTraditions.collector: E. A. Bogacheva, lors d'entretiens menés en 2017
oralTraditions.context: Account reported in Russian in a university thesis

oralTraditions.claim: The Sundiata epic distinguishes two branches of the name: Kamandjan, king of the Kamara of Sibi, known as Dalikimbon, and his cousin Tabon Wana, king of the blacksmith Kamara of Tabon, known as Sinikimbon. It has Sundiata seal a perpetual alliance between the Kamara of Sibi and the Keita of Manding.
oralTraditions.carrier: Djeli Mamadou Kouyaté, griot de Djeliba Koro, près de Siguiri
oralTraditions.collector: Djibril Tamsir Niane, qui l'a traduit en français

oralTraditions.claim: The Kamara praise motto recited in the epic names the Kamara of Sibi, Tabon and Nyengenba, and tells that their grandfather split the rock of Sibi with his sabre, which became the gateway of entry and exit of Kamajan. The editors of the account note that the Traoré and the Kamara are the legendary founders of Kangaba there.
oralTraditions.carrier: Lansine Diabaté, chef de la parole (kumatigi) de Kela, au Mali
oralTraditions.collector: Jan Jansen, Esger Duintjer et Boubacar Tamboura
oralTraditions.context: Account in Maninka published with its French translation in 1995

oralTraditions.claim: Before the Mali empire, the Kamara clan has Sibi and Tabon as its main towns and gradually conquers the right bank of the Niger. The first Niani, said to have been founded by Kamara of Sibi, would lie in the mountains of the left bank between Bamako and Kangaba.
oralTraditions.collector: Djibril Tamsir Niane et Youssouf Tata Cissé, d'après les écoles de tradition orale du Manding
oralTraditions.context: Historical synthesis published by UNESCO in 1985

oralTraditions.claim: The Kamara are presented as the first occupants of several lands of the Manding: at Kita they become allies of Soundiata and remain masters of the land, and local tradition makes Kangaba a foundation of the Kamara of Sibi and the Traoré.
oralTraditions.context: Epic published in 1960 and its notes

oralTraditions.claim: Some Kamara say they descend from Fassuna and Badjuba Nassari, Fassuna being presented as a concubine of the Prophet Muhammad. This account links the name to the household of the Prophet; no other source consulted repeats it.
oralTraditions.collector: Molinie, officier de la marine française, en 1959
oralTraditions.context: Account taken from a dictionary written for Europeans posted in French West Africa, cited at second hand in a 2017 thesis that warns against its unfounded generalisations; the informant is not named

oralTraditions.claim: The Maninka clans that reached the sea near Lake Pisu (Robertsport) and organised the Vai people there are said, according to tradition, to have been led by Kamala the Younger, Fangoloma and Kiatamba; the same tradition is said to confirm that the clans led by the Kamara were related to those of the Konyan. The chiefs are named Kamala, not Kamara. The rest of the journey, its date and its course belong to the historical synthesis of this fiche.
oralTraditions.collector: Yves Person, qui rapporte la tradition sans en nommer les porteurs
oralTraditions.context: Historical synthesis published by UNESCO in 1985

writtenChronicles.claim: The name is said to come from an order given to the first common sovereign of the Sankaran countries: he was told "let him reign!", and the phrase became the name of his descendants. The same work, written in N'ko by Souleymane Kanté, counts six branches of the name: Tabon, Sibi, Gbakundo, Kidimaga, Somono and Fina Kamara.

historicalSyntheses.claim: Historical syntheses have the Camara clan lead a movement of Mandinka clans from the upper Niger towards the coast, giving rise to the Kono and the Vai of Sierra Leone and Liberia, and place Malinké of the Camara clan in Liberia and western Côte d'Ivoire in the sixteenth century, the Diomandé being described as brothers of the Camara. The date of the Kono and Vai movement is disputed: before the 1460s, and perhaps as early as the preceding century, for one author, who relies notably on the closeness of the Kono and Vai languages to Maninka; between 1500 and 1550 for another; possibly several centuries earlier for a third, who finds the image of a rapid incursion led by a single chief unconvincing. For this movement, the first writes Kamara and the second Camara.

linguisticReconstructions.claim: No dictionary or linguist's work consulted gives the word a meaning: the dictionary of Mandinka clan names defines it only as a clan name. The griot who tells the epic published in 1960 claims to know why a person is called Kamara, but does not say.
Among the Vai, the name is pronounced Kamana where the Malinké say Kamara.
One hypothesis has the name appearing first among the ancestors of the Soninké, before the Malinké world. It is put forward as probable, not as established.

A colonial administrator asked in 1907 whether Kamara might come from Hamara, the "red men of the North". The question rests on a resemblance of sounds, in a line of reasoning that seeks a Berber origin for the Mande peoples by comparing their language with Berber.

A historian cited in a UNESCO synthesis sets apart the "Kamara factor" in the origin of the Vai as deserving further research, and considers it useful to establish how far non-Mandinka groups bear Mandinka names. This is an open question.

casteOrSocialFunction.value: The name does not denote a single status. The dictionary of Mandinka clan names gives three statuses for Kàmara: hɔ̀rɔn (free person), finɛ and nùmu (blacksmith) in Wassoulou, and Charry expressly ranks the name among the blacksmith lineages, alongside Kanté. The Sundiata epic likewise separates the Kamara of Sibi, a royal line, from the blacksmith Kamara of Tabon. A study of the griots' jamu also notes Camara who hold the function of griot without being of griot descent. Endogamous groups of artisans and musicians, whose status is transmitted with the name, are attested among the Malinké by around 1300 at the latest.

searchAnswer.lead: A Mandinka clan name, attested notably in Mali, Guinea, Liberia and Côte d'Ivoire.
searchAnswer.followUp: What do the sources say about the presence of the name Camara on the coast, in Liberia and Sierra Leone?

sources.title: EthniAfrica — fiche du peuple Vai, organisation clanique
sources.notes: Taken from the "Clan organisation" chapter of the Vai people's fiche.

sources.title: A Guide to the Jembe
sources.notes: Charry, Eric, Percussive Notes 34(2), April 1996, pp. 66-72; the author is the ethnomusicologist who wrote Mande Music (University of Chicago Press, 2000). A specialist journal article, not a peer-reviewed one: it is cited here for the attribution of jamuw to Mandinka social statuses (numu, jeli, horon), which it states by name, clan by clan, and not for the history of the jembe.

sources.title: The Development of Caste Systems in West Africa
sources.notes: Tamari, Tal, The Journal of African History 32(2), 1991, pp. 221-250; open deposit on HAL-SHS. Establishes that endogamous groups of artisans and musicians are found among more than fifteen West African peoples and that they are attested among the Malinke by around 1300 at the latest. Used for the institution of caste, never to link a named clan to a caste: that attribution comes from another source.

sources.title: Bamadaba — dictionnaire des noms claniques (jamuw)
sources.notes: Appendix of clan names in the Bamadaba, the electronic Bambara-French dictionary of the Corpus bambara de référence (Bailleul, Davydov, Erman, Maslinsky, Méric, Vydrin, 2011-2020, CC BY-NC-SA), pointed out by Vydrin in Mandenkan 63, 2020, pp. 89-110. Complete file consulted. The entry Kàmara gives the variant Kámala, the statuses hɔ̀rɔn, finɛ and nùmu (the last in Wassoulou), the Koiwogi equivalents among the Loma, Dansogo, Fofana and Magasa, and Kuruma, Fofana, Sila and Wulare as joking partners; it gives no meaning for the name. The pairing with Kanté is carried by the entry Kántɛ, not by the entry Kàmara.

sources.title: Relevé de couverture anthroponymique EthniAfrica
sources.notes: List of names kept by EthniAfrica. It records the name in a country without a dedicated source documenting it there: the country is therefore given as presumed, not as attested.

sources.title: Pouvoir, places et filiation : les senankuya au Mali
sources.notes: Canut, Cécile, Cahiers de praxématique, issue 38, 2002, pp. 175-197. Field survey in Mali. It states what the pact requires: the relationship holds in perpetuity for all the descendants of the two lineages, marriage between them is prohibited (applied unevenly today, it notes), and mutual aid is owed without reservation. Cited for the obligation itself; it does not name the pair in this fiche, which is carried by the entries cited alongside it.

sources.title: Pactes, alliances et plaisanteries. Pratiques locales, discours global
sources.notes: Canut, Cécile, and Smith, Étienne, Cahiers d'études africaines, issue 184, 2006, p. 687 ff. Cited for the caution it carries: the idea that joking kinship soothes conflict is treated there as a hypothesis inherited from Radcliffe-Brown and taken up by conflict-resolution studies, hence as a discourse to be analysed and not as a measured effect. The first page is verified; the last page is not.

sources.title: Histoire générale de l'Afrique, IV : L'Afrique du XIIe au XVIe siècle — chapitre 6, Le Mali et la deuxième expansion manden
sources.notes: UNESCO, ed. D. T. Niane, 1985; chapter by D. T. Niane. Printed pages: the Kamara holding Sibi and Tabon and conquering the right bank of the Niger (p. 153), called together with the Keita, Konaté and Traoré by Mamadi Kani (p. 154), Tabon Wana and his cousin Kamajan Kamara of Sibi (p. 155), Niani in Kamara country and the first Niani founded by the Kamara of Sibi, according to a communication by Y. Cissé at the 1975 colloquium of the SCOA Foundation (p. 160, note 47). The chapter gives no meaning for the name and does not cite the Kamara among the clans of the Kurukanfuga assembly. It names no country: Sibi is located there "between Siguiri and Kangaba" (p. 155) and the first Niani "between Bamako and Kangaba" (p. 160, note 47), and it is therefore not cited here as an attestation of the name in a country.

sources.title: Histoire générale de l'Afrique, IV : L'Afrique du XIIe au XVIe siècle — chapitre 12, Les peuples côtiers, premiers contacts avec les Portugais, de la Casamance aux lagunes ivoiriennes
sources.notes: UNESCO, 1985; chapter by Yves Person. Printed pages: the Kamara of the Konyan at the origin of the invasion that reaches the coast of Liberia and Sierra Leone in 1540-1550, put forward as almost certain (p. 341); the Konyan under the hegemony of the Kamara and Dyomande clans, whose legendary ancestor is Feren-Kaman (p. 345); Maninka clans led by the Kamara reaching the sea from the upper Niger, and related, "as tradition confirms", to the clans of the Konyan, established before the 1460s and perhaps as early as the preceding century, this date being given by the author as his own synthesis; the Vai led, "according to tradition", by Kamala the Younger, Fangoloma and Kiatamba (p. 346). Only two elements are given as tradition: the names of the chiefs, which are written Kamala and not Kamara, and the kinship with the clans of the Konyan; the rest of the account, including the date, is the author's synthesis. The chapter does not place the Konyan in Guinea (p. 345: "Konyan and Mau (at Touba, in the Republic of Côte d'Ivoire)") and therefore does not cite the Kamara in that country. For the movement of the Kono and the Vai, it writes Kamara where the chapter by Wondji (General History of Africa, V) writes Camara. It locates the coast near Lake Pisu, on the border of Liberia and Sierra Leone; it does not say that the name is borne in Sierra Leone, which remains assumed here.

sources.title: Histoire générale de l'Afrique, V : L'Afrique du XVIe au XVIIIe siècle — chapitre 13, Les États et les cultures de la côte de haute Guinée
sources.notes: UNESCO, ed. B. A. Ogot, 1999; chapter by C. Wondji. Printed pages: the Kono-Vai coming from the upper Niger at the turn of the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries under the leadership of the Camara clan, by Bopolou and then the Mano and Moa rivers, between 1500 and 1550 according to Holsoe and his co-authors (p. 419); the Malinké of the Camara clan established in the sixteenth century in Liberia and western Côte d'Ivoire, and the Diomandé said to be brothers of the Camara (p. 421). The same chapter places a movement of the Malinké of Konyan in the seventeenth century without naming the Camara (p. 423). It writes Camara where the chapter by Person (General History of Africa, IV) writes Kamara.

sources.title: Histoire générale de l'Afrique, III : L'Afrique du VIIe au XIe siècle — chapitre 18, Les peuples de la Guinée supérieure
sources.notes: UNESCO, ed. M. El Fasi and I. Hrbek, 1990; chapter by B. W. Andah. Printed pages, re-read: an arrival of the Vai in Sierra Leone possible several centuries before the date of 1455 put forward by Person, and the model of a rapid incursion led by a single chief judged unconvincing (p. 590); according to A. Jones, the "Kamara factor" deserves further research, and the use of Mandinka names by non-Mandinka groups would need to be measured (p. 591).

sources.title: Soundjata ou l'épopée mandingue
sources.notes: Niane, Djibril Tamsir, Présence Africaine, 1960. Transcription of the narrative of the griot Djeli Mamadou Kouyaté of Djeliba Koro (Siguiri); it is a written record of an oral tradition. Pages read on the digitised copy on archive.org (SoundjataOuLepopeeMandingue), close to the printed edition without being identical to it: the griot says he knows why someone is called Kamara without saying it (p. 9); Tabon, in the country now called Fouta Djallon, inhabited by the Kamara blacksmiths and the Djallonkés (p. 62); Kamandjan king of the Kamara, called Dalikimbon, and Tabon Wana king of the Kamara blacksmiths, called Sinikimbon (p. 101); the Kamara of Kita allied to Sundiata (p. 129); the alliance of the Kamara of Sibi and the Keita of Manding (p. 140); the Kamara remaining masters of the land (p. 142); Kangaba founded by the Kamara of Sibi and the Traoré according to local tradition (p. 143, note). Pages 9 to 143 cited here were re-read on this copy.

sources.title: L'Épopée de Sunjara, d'après Lansine Diabate de Kela (Mali)
sources.notes: Jansen, Jan, Duintjer, Esger, and Tamboura, Boubacar, CNWS, Leiden, 1995; account by the master of the word Lansine Diabaté of Kela, in Maninka with translation. The motto of the Kamara of Sibi, Tabon and Nyengenba (p. 118, line 344); the split rock of Sibi, gate of Kamajan (p. 183, lines 606-607); editors' note on the Traoré and the Kamara as legendary founders of Kangaba (p. 208, note 199). These pages could not be reopened at the last check (text not accessible): they are reproduced as they stand and remain to be re-read; this source is therefore not used for any country.

sources.title: Les noms de clan du Manden (jamu) dans les sources africaines, occidentales et arabes
sources.notes: Bogacheva, E. A., bachelor's thesis, Saint Petersburg State University, 2017, in Russian; supervised by A. Davydov, reviewed by V. Vydrin. Entry Kàmara, pp. 73-76, read in the copy deposited by the university: the French spellings Camara and Kamara, given for the same clan name (p. 73); Sibi in the Bamako circle, after Molinie, without the page naming a country (p. 74); the hypothesis of a first appearance of the name among the ancestors of the Soninke, after N'Diaye 1970 (p. 74); the account of descent reported by Molinie in 1959 (p. 74); the origin as told in Souleymane Kanté's N'Ko work on the names and jamu of the Manden, and the six branches of the name (p. 75); the account of the griot Babou Condé of Fadama, collected in 2017 (p. 76). The author places these interviews in Fadama, in the Kouroussa circle, during an expedition to Guinea (p. 11): this places the account in Guinea, not the clan. The original N'Ko text by Kanté was not read; only its Russian translation was. A bachelor's thesis is not a peer-reviewed publication: it is cited for the testimonies it transmits.

sources.title: Les Vai : leur langue et leur système d'écriture
sources.notes: Delafosse, Maurice, L'Anthropologie, vol. X, 1899, p. 134 (page 6 of the offprint): "les Kamana (au lieu de Kamara chez les Malinke)". A colonial-era author, cited here for a recorded form, not for his classifications.

sources.title: La Guinée française
sources.notes: Arcin, André, Challamel, 1907, appendix II, pp. 635-636. Colonial administrator. The question about the "red men of the North" (p. 635) precedes a comparison of Mande with Berber (p. 636); it is cited as an example of an explanation coming from outside, not as an etymology. For the presence of the name in Guinea: "the Kamara of Beyla (Konianka) and of the upper regions of Liberia (Manianka)", whom the author says appear to be close relatives of the Diomandé (p. 310, taken from the digitised archive.org text on the basis of the page headers).

sources.title: Les valeurs identitaires du jamu de griot dans Kuyaté la force du serment
sources.notes: Konaté, Diola, Revue d'études africaines, Université Cheikh Anta Diop, issue 2, 2015: Kamara among the jamu of nobles or horon (p. 53); Camara who act as griots without being of griot descent (p. 61). Study of a literary work by Drissa Diakité.

gaps.reason: A 2017 master's thesis on the clan names of the Manden gives Camara and Kamara as two French spellings of the same clan name, Kàmara; it is the only source read that links them, and it does not say which of the two came first. The dictionary of Mandinka clan names, like the thesis, adds Kámala and gives as equivalents, held to be the same clan under other names, Koiwogi among the Loma, as well as Dansogo (written Dansoko in the thesis), Fofana and Magasa; the thesis adds Mara and Sekonho among the Senufo. The sources read present them as spellings and equivalences, not as distinct lineages. We have found no source that distinguishes the Mandinka name from the Portuguese or Spanish name Câmara, borne elsewhere for other reasons.
